current_episode.title: Behind the Scenes on Broadway: What a Stage Manager Really Does

guest.bio_context: Billy worked on Broadway for 30 years before retiring with a substantial pension. He began his theater career in high school performing in The Sound of Music, then studied theater at State University of New York at Fredonia where he learned all aspects of theatrical production. He transitioned from performing to stage management after becoming frustrated with the life of an actor, starting as a stage manager for acting class readings before becoming a professional stage manager on Broadway productions.

How I got into it non-professionally was I did theater in high school. I was attracted to it from seventh grade when I was in a production of The Sound of Music. I played one of the kids. I was hooked. In high school, in order to be in the productions, we had to work backstage. We had to work on Saturdays. We had something called work parties, and we would work on sets, costumes, props, putting the show together, mainly building the sets. And in that process of doing that and then And being on stage, I developed this awareness of not only what it was like to be a performer, but what it took to create the stage and the lights and the props and the costumes and wigs and everything that it took behind the scenes. Was your dream to be a performer? Yes, yes. That was my dream to be a performer and to be a star on Broadway or a rock star. I wasn't picky. I just wanted to be a star. And so I went to school for music for one semester, and then I switched to theater because I was a singer too. And in university settings, first one was a state university and the second one was a private university, part of your requirement when you're a performer is to work backstage and to work in the shops and learn how to not only build shows but run shows, run lights, run follow spots, run carpentry queues on the deck. You learn all that in university settings. Sometimes it's very divided. In my case, the school I went to, which was State University of New York at Fredonia, everybody did everything, just like my high school. So it was just kind of like a carryover. And I would get on crews of shows, and I was performing in shows. But the thing that even always when I was performing, I was always aware of that it wasn't just me up there with the audience and my fellow actors, that there was a whole infrastructure backstage that was kind of allowing us to be there and for the show to be effective. And then I went to New York. I was waiting tables, doing kind of theater as a hobby. But I was in a lot of productions. They just didn't really pay me anything. And at a certain... You were in production as a performer or as a stage manager? As a performer. And at a certain point, I started to get a little frustrated with the life of an actor. You're only as good as your last audition. You can be fabulous in a show and everybody can love you. You can walk into an audition and they may love you. And then they'll say, yeah, but you're just not right for this show. And I just got sick of hearing that. So I was taking acting classes. They were doing some readings and the director needed a stage manager for it. And basically what he needed was to schedule people's availabilities around their work schedules. pending_qa.q: How much can a stage manager earn on Broadway versus other theater venues?
pending_qa.r: On Broadway, the union minimum contract for a production stage manager is $4,000 a week. If working on a hit show like Book of Mormon, Wicked, or Hamilton, stage managers can earn $200,000 a year plus pension contributions, health insurance, and 401k contributions. In regional theaters, off-Broadway, and smaller productions, pay is considerably less, potentially a quarter of the Broadway salary. Freelance theater gigs can pay as little as $1,000 for four weeks of rehearsals and performances.

pending_qa.q: What major Broadway and off-Broadway productions has Billy worked on?
pending_qa.r: Billy worked on Hello Dolly, Love Valor Compassion (which won a Tony for best play), Masterclass (Tony winner for best play), Art (Tony winner for best play), Take Me Out, a revival of Glengarry Glen Ross with Liev Schreiber and Alan Alda, a revival of A View from the Bridge with Scarlett Johansson, and the first Broadway production of Three Days of Rain with Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd, and Bradley Cooper. He also worked on Hair during a tour.

pending_qa.q: What are the biggest challenges of working as a stage manager?
pending_qa.r: The biggest challenge is the schedule: stage managers work eight shows a week, six days a week, and are on call 24/7. They must be ready to handle emergencies like actors falling ill or being injured, theater flooding, or technical failures during performances. There is also significant job insecurity, with gaps between shows where stage managers may need to work restaurant jobs to pay bills and living expenses.

pending_qa.q: How can someone with no theater experience break into stage management?
pending_qa.r: Billy recommends getting backstage on a show through community theater, high school drama club, college theater departments, or regional theater by volunteering. He emphasizes that volunteering is often necessary when starting out since entry-level theater work pays little or nothing. He stresses that seeing theater as an audience is very different from being backstage doing the work, so hands-on experience is essential.

pending_qa.q: What personal qualities and skills are essential to succeed as a stage manager?
pending_qa.r: A stage manager must love theater, not be afraid to get hands dirty, and embrace the collaborative process of putting shows together. They must check their ego because they work with many artists who are vulnerable performers taking risks on stage. They need to be willing to support other artists in the room, be organizationally skilled, handle stress well, and if working on Broadway, possess enough artistic ambition to reach the level of professional stage manager.

pending_qa.q: What are the financial rewards beyond salary for long-term Broadway stage managers?
pending_qa.r: Beyond the $200,000 annual salary on hit shows, stage managers benefit from union pension plans that provide substantial retirement income. Billy retired with a considerable pension after 30 years on Broadway. The union also provides health insurance and allows producers to contribute dedicated money to 401k accounts, creating a comprehensive benefits package.

pending_qa.q: How do stage managers handle unexpected emergencies during live performances?
pending_qa.r: If technical problems occur during a show, the stage manager must decide whether to stop the performance or continue. If stopping is necessary, the stage manager makes an announcement to the audience explaining the interruption. Billy has had to stop shows for technical issues, medical emergencies like audience members having heart attacks, and for actors getting seriously injured, sometimes requiring understudies to be brought in quickly.
